title: Saccaka's boast
hookLine: a well-known debater boasts he will shake the Buddha, and sweats instead

cards: In the city of Vesali lives a debater named Saccaka, and he is very good. He says so himself. There's no teacher alive, he tells crowds, who wouldn't shake and tremble if he debated them.
Even a post, he says, would shake if he argued with it, never mind a human being. Then he hears what the Buddha teaches, and announces he'll drag him around like a man dragging a sheep by its fleece.
Five hundred people come to watch.

teach.h: THE BODY IS MY SELF, SAYS SACCAKA
teach.b: This is the shorter discourse to Saccaka, the thirty-fifth of the Middle-Length Sayings. Saccaka opens: the body is my self, and so are feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness.
The Buddha doesn't argue back at once. He asks a question.

teach.h: A KING RULES; CAN YOU RULE YOUR BODY?
teach.b: A king rules his country; can he have someone executed, fined or banished? Of course, says Saccaka.
Then you say the body is your self. Can you command it: let my body be like this, don't let it be like that? Saccaka goes silent.
The Buddha asks again. Silence again. The text adds a dramatic touch: a spirit named Vajirapani hovers above with a thunderbolt, and only Saccaka and the Buddha can see him.
The Buddha asks a third time, and Saccaka answers: no. I can't command it. Then the same for feeling, perception, formations, consciousness.
If it can't be commanded, and it changes, and it brings pain when it changes, is it fit to call it mine, I, my self? No.

teach.h: SWEAT ON HIS ROBE, NONE ON THE BUDDHA
teach.b: At the end, sweat pours from Saccaka's forehead, soaks through his robe and drips to the ground. The Buddha notes, gently, that there's no sweat on his own body.
And someone in the crowd says Saccaka looks like a crab with its legs broken, unable to crawl back into its pond. But Saccaka isn't a villain.
He invites the Buddha and the monks to a meal the next day, and later comes back for another talk, which we hear tomorrow.
Certainty that has never been tested can sweat when it finally is.

how: Buddhist teachers use MN 35's question, whether we can command the body and mind to be as we wish, as a classic way into the teaching of not-self (anatta) and the five aggregates.

o: a debater's brag, undone by one question
a monk's vow to win every argument
a king's victory speech after a battle

games.q: the debate in Vesali — tap the pairs.
p: even a post would shake before me
can't be commanded to be thus
how Saccaka looked at the end

s: the Buddha won by out-arguing Saccaka point by point
he asked a question: can you command your body to be as you wish? Saccaka's silence did the rest.
Saccaka sweated through his robe while the Buddha didn't sweat
the text says Saccaka's sweat dripped to the ground, and the Buddha's body had none.
Saccaka left angry and never came back
he invited the Buddha to a meal, and returned for another conversation in MN 36.

games.q: you're Saccaka. the Buddha asks: can you command your body, 'let it be like this, not like that'? five hundred people are watching. what do you do?
o: change the subject to the weather.
games.why: Saccaka stays silent twice. asked a third time, he admits: no. then the sweat starts.

practice: Try the Buddha's question on yourself: tell your body, don't let this knee ache, don't let my mind wander, and watch the next minute.
Notice the body and mind doing what they do, commanded or not, and if a little thought of I'm good at this shows up, let it pass too, like Saccaka's crowd going home.

wordCard.voice: Saccaka's boast. The debater who said even a post would shake before him, and ended up sweating, then coming back for more.

carryVoice: Your line: the sweat of certainty. Even Saccaka came back for more. That's day four hundred thirty.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 35, Culasaccaka Sutta (the shorter discourse to Saccaka)
Samyutta Nikaya 22.59, Anattalakkhana Sutta (the characteristic of not-self)
